meta.title: The Parameterized Scheduling Zoo
meta.note: Seed dataset for prototyping the site. Entries marked "confidence": "verified" reflect well-known landmark results; entries marked "illustrative" are plausible placeholders standing in for real results and should be checked against the literature before being trusted. Classical α|β|γ notation follows Graham, Lawler, Lenstra & Rinnooy Kan (1979).

classicalClasses.label: weakly NP-hard
classicalClasses.description: NP-hard, and a pseudo-polynomial-time algorithm is known.

classicalClasses.label: NP-hard (weak/strong open)
classicalClasses.description: Known NP-hard, but whether it is strongly NP-hard or admits a pseudo-polynomial algorithm is open.

classicalClasses.label: strongly NP-hard
classicalClasses.description: NP-hard even when all numeric input is given in unary; no pseudo-polynomial algorithm unless P=NP.

classicalClasses.label: open
classicalClasses.description: Not even known to be NP-hard; complexity status unsettled.

complexityClasses.label: FPT
complexityClasses.description: Fixed-parameter tractable: solvable in f(k)·poly(n) time.

complexityClasses.label: XP
complexityClasses.description: Solvable in n^f(k) time; not known to be FPT.

complexityClasses.label: W[1]-hard
complexityClasses.description: W[1]-hard: unlikely to be FPT under standard assumptions.

complexityClasses.label: W[2]-hard
complexityClasses.description: W[2]-hard: unlikely to be FPT (stronger than W[1]).

complexityClasses.label: para-NP-hard
complexityClasses.description: NP-hard even for a constant value of the parameter.

complexityClasses.label: open
complexityClasses.description: Complexity status not known / not settled.

parameters.name: number of machines
parameters.gloss: The number of machines in the scheduling instance, taken as a parameter instead of part of the input size. Many problems that are NP-hard for arbitrary m turn out to be FPT or remain hard when m is small and fixed.

parameters.name: maximum processing time
parameters.gloss: The largest job processing time in the instance. Parameterizing by p_max turns pseudo-polynomial dynamic programs (which run in time polynomial in the numeric value of processing times) into FPT algorithms.

parameters.name: number of distinct processing times
parameters.gloss: The number of distinct values that appear among job processing times. Small #p lets jobs be grouped into few interchangeable classes, which is the basis of n-fold integer programming approaches.

parameters.name: number of distinct weights
parameters.gloss: The number of distinct job weight values. Analogous in spirit to #p, but for weights instead of processing times.

parameters.name: number of distinct release dates
parameters.gloss: The number of distinct release-date values. Small #r lets jobs be grouped by release-date class.

parameters.name: number of distinct machine speeds
parameters.gloss: The number of distinct machine speed values in a uniform-machines (Q) environment.

parameters.name: treewidth of the precedence graph
parameters.gloss: The treewidth of the DAG describing precedence constraints between jobs. Bounded treewidth typically enables dynamic programming over a tree decomposition.

parameters.name: vertex cover number of the precedence graph
parameters.gloss: The size of a minimum vertex cover of the (underlying undirected) precedence graph — i.e. the number of jobs whose removal leaves no precedence edges.

problems.name: Single machine, makespan
problems.classicalStatus: Trivially polynomial (schedule all jobs back to back in any order).
problems.overview: The base case of the base case: with one machine and no constraints, makespan is fixed the moment job processing times are fixed, independent of the schedule chosen. It sits at the root of the zoo mostly as a sanity check for the interface, and as the natural starting point when adding constraints such as release dates or precedence.

problems.name: Identical parallel machines, makespan
problems.overview: The classic multiprocessor scheduling problem: given jobs with processing times and m identical machines, minimize the time the last job finishes. NP-hard already for m=2 (it encodes Partition), but its pseudo-polynomial dynamic program is the textbook example of how a numeric parameter (p_max) or a structural one (m, #p) can turn intractability into fixed-parameter tractability.

results.note: Encode as an ILP whose number of variables depends only on m; solvable in f(m)·poly(n) time via Lenstra's algorithm for integer programming in fixed dimension.
The classic O(n·m·p_max) subset-sum-style dynamic program is already FPT when p_max is taken as the parameter.
Group jobs by processing time and use an n-fold integer programming formulation whose dimension depends on #p and m.
Placeholder — not meaningful for identical machines; included to show how an 'open' cell renders.

problems.name: Unrelated machines, makespan
problems.overview: Each job may take a different amount of time on each machine. Lenstra, Shmoys & Tardos gave the classic 2-approximation and showed exact solution is strongly NP-hard; the parameterized picture asks which structural restrictions (few machines, few distinct processing times) restore tractability.

results.note: FPT via a Lenstra-type ILP algorithm; the parameter m bounds the number of integer variables needed to encode an optimal assignment.
Listed as an open direction in the Mnich & van Bevern survey; whether the problem is FPT in p_max alone is not settled in this seed dataset.

problems.name: Uniform machines, makespan
problems.overview: Machines run at different but job-independent speeds. It sits between P||Cmax and R||Cmax in generality, and the parameterized results largely mirror P||Cmax with an added parameter for machine-speed diversity.

results.note: Same ILP-in-fixed-dimension argument as P||Cmax, generalized to account for machine speeds.
Group machines by speed class; the resulting n-fold IP dimension depends on #speeds and m.

problems.name: Identical machines with precedence constraints, makespan
problems.classicalStatus: NP-hard for general m; already hard for m=2 with arbitrary processing times.
problems.overview: Adding precedence constraints to identical-machine scheduling is a textbook example of a problem that gets harder, not easier, to parameterize: while P||Cmax is FPT in the number of machines m, adding precedence pushes that same parameterization to W[2]-hard. It is the canonical illustration that structural parameters interact with side constraints in ways that raw problem size doesn't.

results.note: Landmark hardness result: adding precedence constraints pushes the m-parameterization from FPT (identical/unrelated machines without precedence) to W[2]-hard.
Bounded-treewidth precedence DAGs admit a dynamic program that tracks a bounded-size frontier of the tree decomposition.

problems.name: Single machine, release dates, total completion time
problems.overview: Minimizing total completion time is trivial without release dates (shortest processing time first), but adding release dates makes even the single-machine case strongly NP-hard. The natural parameters here count distinct release-date or processing-time values rather than machines, since there is only one machine.

results.note: Jobs sharing a release date form interchangeable blocks; the state space of a DP depends only on the number of distinct release dates.

problems.name: Single machine, weighted number of tardy jobs
problems.overview: Deciding which jobs to let be late (rather than by how much) turns this into a knapsack-flavored problem: the on-time jobs must fit before their due dates, and among feasible on-time sets we maximize completed weight. Distinct-value parameters (#w, #p) are the natural knobs since they bound the number of interchangeable job classes.

results.note: With few distinct weight classes, an ILP/DP of dimension depending on #w becomes tractable.
Solvable in n^f(#p) time via brute-force over per-class schedules; not known whether this can be improved to FPT.

problems.name: Two-machine open shop, makespan
problems.overview: Open-shop scheduling with two machines is one of the few multi-operation shop-scheduling problems solvable exactly in polynomial time, via a simple list-scheduling argument. It's included mainly as a green, parameter-independent baseline for contrast against the harder shop-scheduling variants.

problems.name: 3-stage flow shop, weighted number of non-JIT jobs
problems.overview: Zj = 1 if job j does not complete exactly on its due date (a just-in-time / JIT objective), 0 otherwise; ΣwjZj is the weighted count of jobs that miss their exact due date. With three sequential stages and general weights this is strongly NP-hard — the top of this generalization family.

problems.name: 3-stage flow shop, number of non-JIT jobs
problems.overview: The unweighted (wj=1) special case of F3||ΣwjZj. Still strongly NP-hard — unlike the 2-stage case, dropping weights does not restore polynomial-time solvability once a third stage is added.

problems.name: Flexible flow shop (1 machine, then m parallel machines), weighted number of non-JIT jobs
problems.classicalStatus: NP-hard; strong/weak status and pseudo-polynomial solvability open.
problems.overview: A 2-stage flexible flow shop: every job first passes through a single machine, then through one of m identical parallel machines. Generalizes P||ΣwjZj (by adding stage 1) and specializes into F(1,c)||ΣwjZj when the second-stage machine count is bounded by a constant c.

problems.name: Flexible flow shop (1 machine, then c parallel machines, c constant), weighted number of non-JIT jobs
problems.overview: Same 2-stage flexible flow shop as F(1,m)||ΣwjZj, but with the second-stage machine count fixed to a constant c rather than left arbitrary. Bounding the machine count resolves the open weak/strong question of F(1,m): here a pseudo-polynomial algorithm is known. Setting c=1 degenerates to the plain 2-stage flow shop F2||ΣwjZj.

problems.name: 2-stage flow shop, weighted number of non-JIT jobs
problems.overview: The c=1 special case of F(1,c)||ΣwjZj, and the 2-stage special case of F3||ΣwjZj. Dropping weights (Zj unweighted) restores polynomial solvability; dropping a stage (down to 1 machine) also restores polynomial solvability.

problems.name: 2-stage flow shop, number of non-JIT jobs
problems.overview: The unweighted special case of F2||ΣwjZj. Unlike the 3-stage case, dropping weights here does restore polynomial-time solvability — the weight axis and the stage-count axis interact rather than acting independently.

problems.name: Identical parallel machines, weighted number of non-JIT jobs
problems.overview: The parallel-machines axis: this is the 1||ΣwjZj problem generalized by allowing m identical machines instead of one, and itself the special case of F(1,m)||ΣwjZj where stage-1 processing times are all zero.

problems.name: Single machine, weighted number of non-JIT jobs
problems.overview: The base case of this family: a single machine, general weights. Polynomial, and the common ancestor that both the parallel-machines axis (→P||ΣwjZj) and the flow-shop axis (→F2||ΣwjZj→F3||ΣwjZj) generalize from.

problems.name: Single machine, number of non-JIT jobs
problems.overview: The simplest problem in the family: one machine, unit weights. Polynomial, as are all of its direct generalizations along a single axis (adding machines or an extra unweighted flow-shop stage) — it only takes a combination of axes to reach NP-hardness.

maps.title: JIT Flow Shop
maps.description: Weighted number of just-in-time-violating jobs, across three independent generalization axes: number of flow-shop stages, flexibility (parallel machines at a stage), and weighted vs. unweighted.
